To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

water conservation policies are unlikely to reduce irrigation water depletions in a basin with limited water supply, unless they are designed to target water depletions, and not water diversions or water applications.

(1) conservation subsidies do not reduce water use in irrigation; (2) conservation subsidies reduce aquifer recharge; and (3) conservation programs that target reduced diversions or applications do not save water.
(1) water conservation policies can increase water use in irrigated agriculture and (2) water conservation subsidies do not necessarily reduce water use.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: Can water be conserved in irrigation? The answer is yes, if water conservation programs target reduced water depletion, and if they are designed to reward water conservation.

conservation is not always conservation.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the water conservation policy debate needs to move beyond a focus on water applications and diversions to one that focuses on water depletion and recharge.
the effects of water conservation policies depend critically on the institutional and technical conditions that prevail in a particular basin.
